subject: Pilot throughput checklist and streaming latency gaps
messages:
From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.com>
To: Samir Patel <samir@quickdeliver.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 18 Jun 2028 14:02:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: QuickDeliver pilot — throughput checklist and open latency items

Hi Samir / Alicia — thanks for the time today. Follow-up notes from our call focused on the pilot sizing and two streaming-related latency items we want to lock down before we hand off to Docs & SREs. Summary below plus immediate asks.

Quick summary of what we heard from you on the call:
- Primary workload: real-time route suggestions inside driver app (streaming single-turn requests, partial tokens streamed back as suggestions)
- Burst profile: ~3.5k concurrent drivers during peak dispatch windows (~1800-2000 QPS equivalent for short requests)
- Steady profile: ~600 concurrent drivers outside rush windows (~320 QPS)
- Typical request size: 40–120 tokens in, 30–60 tokens out (average 80 tokens round-trip)
- Latency target: drivers require visible suggestions in 300–500ms for the first partial chunk, with full completion ideally < 1.5s for short flows

Assumptions we're using for initial sizing (please confirm or correct):
- Tokenization mapping: 1 token ~= 4 characters -> will validate against your sample logs
- Average server-side processing time per token at baseline quantized model (fp16/8-bit): 0.7–1.2ms/token depending on batch sizing
- Streaming chunking: we should plan for 16–32 token partial chunks to hit the perceptual latency target

Immediate asks (can you send before EOD Wednesday):
1) A 48–72 hour sample of request telemetry (timestamps, request length, response length, user-region) — you can drop the file as CSV (ops@quickdeliver.com to redwood-sharing).
2) Confirmation of 95th and 99th percentile mobile network RTTs observed during peak windows (US west regions) — helps set headroom for client-to-edge and edge-to-server.

Planned next steps from Redwood if we get the telemetry:
- Marissa will run a quick tokenization pass and return a normalized tokens/sec profile (expected back in 24 business hours).
- Ben will generate a baseline throughput matrix (QPS vs concurrency vs expected token/sec) and propose a Dedicated pilot capacity bucket.
- Karthik will enumerate streaming chunk sizes and propose a fallback policy (partial results vs final) to meet the 300–500ms first-chunk SLO.

Attachments: I attached a short sample CSV template for telemetry and our sizing matrix skeleton (redwood-sizing-matrix.xlsx).

Thanks — we'll treat this as the working set for the pilot scope.

— Hannah
Hannah Schmitt
Product Manager, Performance 
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-demo: QuickDeliver pilot — throughput checklist and open latency items

Hannah — appreciate the clear notes. Quick answers inline: 

On observed workload:
- Confirming peak concurrent drivers: 3.4–3.8k (our sample window hit 3.6k for the 15-minute push)
- Your conversion to QPS looks right for short requests; the client batches requests when route updates overlap, so QPS can spike for 30–45s windows

Request sizes and tokenization:
- We'll run your CSV template against our logs and send back anonymized telemetry by Wed EOD. Expect ~150MB gzipped for 72h — is that ok?

Latency figures:
- Mobile RTT: 95th ~180ms, 99th ~340ms (west coast) during peak; inland/regional nodes can be higher.
- App-side processing is small (<40ms) so most of the headroom has to come from the server and initial transport.

One wrinkle: we have a hard in-app threshold where anything >800ms for first partial chunk degrades UX severely. We can tolerate occasional misses but want 95% of first-chunk events <500ms.

Attachments: I’m attaching a sanitized sample of request logs as qd-telemetry-sample.csv.gz (ops will upload to your sharing link).

Next asks for Redwood: can you provide a short table with the following columns so we can map to our infra ops playbook?
- expected QPS at 99th percentile burst
- recommended concurrency per GPU instance for streaming flows
- recommended initial model quantization and fallback model family

— Samir
Samir Patel
Head of Platform Engineering

Subject: Re: Post-demo: QuickDeliver pilot — throughput checklist and open latency items

Thanks Samir — getting the gzipped telemetry is perfect. Hannah / team, taking this action: I ran a quick back-of-envelope using the call numbers and Samir’s RTTs. High-level table below (we’ll formalize after tokenization of the logs).

High-level recommended starting pilot config (ballpark):
- Expected steady QPS: 300–350 (matches your steady 320 QPS)
- Expected short-burst QPS (15–45s windows): plan capacity for 2,200–2,400 QPS to cover 99th bursts after client batching
- Token-rate assumption for compute sizing: 85 tokens per end-to-end request (40 in, 45 out average) -> tokens/sec aggregate = QPS * 85
- Suggested concurrency per GPU for streaming (NVIDIA H100 quantized path): 180–220 concurrent streaming sessions per GPU (depends on chunk size)

Latency headroom notes (to hit your 95% first-chunk <500ms):
- Client RTT 95th (180ms) + edge handoff 30–50ms + server first-chunk processing target < 220ms = ~430ms (OK)
- For 99th RTT (340ms) we need more headroom; propose partial mitigation with smaller first-chunk sizes and adaptive client buffering during known rush windows

Model & fallback: start with a 8-bit quantized medium-size family (good perf/cost tradeoff). Fallback family = a smaller quantized model to preserve latency during sustained extreme bursts (auto-route by policy).

Ben is generating the full QPS -> tokens/sec -> GPU count matrix and will attach later today. Karthik will propose a streaming-chunk config with progressive decoding sizes: 16 token first-chunk, then 32 token increments.

Next steps (internal):
- Ben to produce redwood-sizing-matrix.xlsx updated with 99th burst profile by 10:30 PT.
- Hannah to validate tokenization mapping once CSV is ingested.
- Karthik to sketch the fallback routing policy and fallback-choice impact on throughput and per-token cost.

Samir — we’ll upload the sizing matrix and a short note explaining the mapping to HubSpot deal QD-4312. Expect links in the next email.

— Marissa

Samir / team — attached is the initial sizing matrix (redwood-sizing-matrix.xlsx) and a very short notes file outlining the assumptions. Key rows called out: steady vs burst, tokens/sec mapping, and recommended Dedicated bucket for pilot. Pulling highlights here: 

Sizing highlights:
- Steady window: 320 QPS * 85 tokens = 27,200 tokens/sec -> recommended 2x H100 (quantized path) with autoscale headroom to 3x for growth
- 15–45s burst window (recommend planning for 2,400 QPS): 2,400 * 85 = 204,000 tokens/sec -> recommended baseline Dedicated pool 12x H100 with fast autoscale to 16x for observed 99th bursts
- Concurrency math: estimated 200 concurrent streaming sessions per GPU (16-token first-chunk) -> aligns to the GPU counts above

Latency mitigations we recommend initially:
- First-chunk = 16 tokens -> reduces per-request processing and improves observed first-byte latency by ~35–45% in our benchmarks
- Adaptive chunking for detected >90th percentile burst windows (client side increase to 8-token chunks so we can parallelize on fewer GPUs)
- Use prefix/KV cache for repeated route context to shave ~0.2–0.4ms/token for common repeated queries

Action items for this thread:
- I uploaded redwood-sizing-matrix.xlsx to the Drive link Marissa referenced and added a tab with both 95th and 99th burst scenarios.
- Hannah: once you confirm the tokenization pass, I’ll re-run the matrix on exact tokens/sec and push a final capacity recommendation.

Samir — two quick clarifying asks so we can finalize by EOD tomorrow:
1) Confirm you are comfortable with the recommended Dedicated starting pool (12x H100 with autoscale to 16x) for the pilot’s burst coverage.
2) Confirm whether the app-level hard threshold for first-chunk at 800ms is a firm blocker or a warning we should treat as a 99.9% constraint.

Ben Carter
Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
